title: Quiet Diplomacy
text:
Diplomats frequently prefer quiet negotiation to public confrontation. A ministry may convey its concerns through private channels, allowing both parties to retreat without losing face. Such discretion is not a sign of weakness; it reflects a calculation that sustained relationships are worth more than a single dramatic gesture. Nevertheless, the public often interprets silence as indifference.

This tension became evident when two neighbouring states sought to resolve a long-standing dispute over fishing rights. Initial talks were conducted behind closed doors, and only once a framework had been agreed did officials acknowledge the discussions. Critics argued that the process excluded fishing communities altogether, while supporters maintained that premature publicity would have destroyed any chance of compromise.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what do diplomats frequently prefer?
According to paragraph two, what was agreed before officials acknowledged the discussions?
What can be inferred about the public's reaction to silence in diplomacy?
options: They may wrongly read silence as indifference
They prefer dramatic gestures to any negotiation

questions.text: What does the writer suggest about the fishing communities?
options: They were fully represented in the talks
They may have been left out of the process

a direct and often hostile meeting or clash between opposing sides

paragraph_translations: Los diplomáticos suelen preferir la negociación discreta a la confrontación pública. Un ministerio puede transmitir sus preocupaciones por canales privados, lo que permite a ambas partes retirarse sin perder la cara. Esa discreción no es señal de debilidad; refleja el cálculo de que las relaciones sostenidas valen más que un solo gesto dramático. Sin embargo, el público suele interpretar el silencio como indiferencia.

Esta tensión se hizo evidente cuando dos Estados vecinos quisieron resolver una disputa antigua sobre los derechos de pesca. Las primeras conversaciones se llevaron a cabo a puerta cerrada, y solo cuando se acordó un marco los funcionarios reconocieron las discusiones. Los críticos sostenían que el proceso excluyó por completo a las comunidades pesqueras, mientras que los partidarios afirmaban que una publicidad prematura habría destruido cualquier posibilidad de compromiso.
